title: p-values are not posterior probabilities
dek: P(data this extreme | H₀) is not P(H₀ | data). A confidence interval’s coverage is not a posterior probability that θ sits in today’s interval. Different questions, both legal.
story: A p-value answers: if this null sampling model were true, how often would a chosen discrepancy be this large or larger? It conditions on H₀ and randomises over hypothetical data. A posterior probability answers: given these data and a prior on θ (or on hypotheses), how to reweight those hypotheses? It conditions on the data and randomises over θ. Switching the conditioner is the inverse-probability error.

A 95% confidence interval is a procedure with a coverage claim: in 95% of hypothetical replications, the random interval contains the fixed θ. Today’s interval either contains θ or it does not. A 95% credible interval is a posterior set with probability 0.95 under p(θ | y). Those can numerically coincide in happy Gaussian–Gaussian problems. They are still not the same sentence.

You may prefer tests, or you may prefer posteriors. What you may not do is caption a p = 0.04 as “4% chance H₀ is true,” or a p > 0.05 as “95% chance the null holds.” The p-value glossary and the credible-interval glossary sit nearby so that this plate can stay a comparison.
deepTitle: When they numerically agree, and when they must not
deep: Lindley’s paradox: in large n, a point-null H₀ can have a large posterior probability while a classical test rejects. Point masses on a precise H₀ and sampling-theory tests are asking different questions at different resolutions.
Bernstein–von Mises: under regularity, posterior intervals and Wald intervals agree approximately. That is a theorem about limits, not a reason to skip the prior in small n or on a boundary.
P-values do not use a prior. That is a feature for some regulatory tests and a bug if you actually have a prior (historical FQ-R rates, a catalogue grade). Write the prior if you use it.
Posterior predictive p-values exist and are not ordinary tail probabilities under a simple H₀. Do not mix the names.
Reporting both: a likelihood (or LRT) plus a posterior with a named prior is honest. Averaging them into one “significance” is not.

example.title: p = 0.04 is not 4%
example.setup: A one-sided test of π = 0.10 versus π > 0.10 yields p = 0.04. A reader writes “there is only a 4% chance the true rate is 10%.” A Bayesian colleague had put a Beta(2, 9) prior on π (mean 0.18) and finds P(π ≤ 0.10 | y) ≈ 0.22.

steps.title: Translate the p-value
steps.body: p = 0.04 says: under π = 0.10, a tail this large happens about 4% of the time. It does not put 4% mass on the point 0.10.

steps.title: Translate the posterior
steps.body: P(π ≤ 0.10 | y) ≈ 0.22 uses a prior that already doubted 0.10 a little and the same likelihood. Different question, different number. Neither number is wrong; the caption was.

steps.title: What to print together
steps.body: Report π̂, an interval (CI or credible, named), and if you test, the H₀, the tail, and α. Do not convert p into a posterior odds without a prior.

example.takeaway: Freeze H₀ and vary Y, or freeze y and vary θ. Do not caption one as the other.

choices: Under the specified H₀ and discrepancy, data this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
The posterior odds of H₀ are 3:97
check.answer: Under the specified H₀ and discrepancy, data this extreme or more would occur about 3% of the time
check.why: The conditioner is H₀, not the hypothesis given the data.

whyWrong.P(H₀ | data) = 0.03: That is a posterior, which needs a prior.
whyWrong.The posterior odds of H₀ are 3:97: Odds require priors and a Bayes factor.
whyWrong.The Type II error is 0.03: Type II is at an alternative, and is not p.

check.prompt: A 95% CI from a long-run procedure with exact 95% coverage. After seeing (0.10, 0.22), P(θ ∈ (0.10, 0.22) | y) in the sampling-theory reading is:
choices: either 0 or 1 (the interval hit or missed the fixed θ); 0.95 was a property of the procedure, not of this realised interval
check.answer: either 0 or 1 (the interval hit or missed the fixed θ); 0.95 was a property of the procedure, not of this realised interval
check.why: Coverage is a probability over hypothetical data, before you freeze y. A posterior would give a number in (0,1) for this interval only after a prior.

whyWrong.0.95 by definition of confidence: That is the most common caption error.
whyWrong.0.05: That is α, not a posterior of this interval.

check.prompt: On the nested plate, “same f(y|θ), opposite freeze” means:
check.figureHint: Reduced box freezes H₀; full box freezes y.
choices: Sampling-theory and Bayesian readings share the sampling model but freeze opposite arguments — data versus parameter
You must use both at once or neither is valid
Priors are sampling distributions of Ȳ
check.answer: Sampling-theory and Bayesian readings share the sampling model but freeze opposite arguments — data versus parameter
check.why: The likelihood function is the shared bridge. The freeze is the culture.

whyWrong.You must use both at once or neither is: Each is valid for its question.
whyWrong.Priors are sampling distributions of Ȳ: Priors live on θ; sampling laws live on estimators.
